about: One entry per rule code of Risk.RULES. The quick check reads the in-scope entries: a hypothesis, the questions that decide it, and the named mitigations a verdict must report on. Reliability wording only.

handoff-after-ack.hypothesis: Work is handed to an in-process thread after the caller gets its answer; a restart loses it and nobody retries.
handoff-after-ack.check: Does the submitted work matter to the business (not a notification or a metric)? Is the caller answered before the work is durable? Does anything re-derive the work later?

mitigations.name: future joined before response
mitigations.text: the future is joined or awaited before the response is returned

mitigations.name: durable claim before fork
mitigations.text: the work was persisted with a claimable state before the submit, and a sweeper or scheduler picks it up

mitigations.name: persistent job runner
mitigations.text: the executor is a persistent job runner (db-scheduler, JobRunr, Quartz with a JDBC store)

mitigations.name: partial sweeper
mitigations.text: a durable claim exists but the sweeper covers only part of the work

mitigations.name: best-effort by owner
mitigations.text: the code states the work is best effort (a comment, a name or a log that says so)

handoff-after-ack.cite: the submit line; the line that answers the caller; the line that proves or disproves the durable claim
handoff-after-ack.fix: Persist the work as a pending row in the same transaction and let a scheduled sweeper process pending rows, or do the work before answering.
handoff-after-ack.verify: Stop the JVM between the response and the task; after a restart the work must still happen.

handoff-after-consume.hypothesis: The consumer hands work to an in-process thread and returns, so the message is acknowledged before the work is done; a restart loses it and the broker never redelivers.
handoff-after-consume.check: Does the forked work matter to the business? When is the message acknowledged (auto-ack on return, manual ack)? Does anything re-derive the work later?

mitigations.name: ack after forked work
mitigations.text: the listener acknowledges manually only after the forked work completes

mitigations.name: durable claim before fork
mitigations.text: the work was persisted with a claimable state before the submit, and a sweeper picks it up

mitigations.name: partial sweeper
mitigations.text: a durable claim exists but the sweeper covers only part of the work

handoff-after-consume.cite: the submit line; the listener method's return or ack; the line that proves or disproves a durable claim
handoff-after-consume.fix: Do the work on the listener thread before returning, or persist it as a pending row and process it with a sweeper.
handoff-after-consume.verify: Deliver a message and stop the JVM before the forked task runs; after a restart the work must still happen.

async-in-tx.hypothesis: A task is submitted before the transaction commits; it can run before the data is visible, or after a rollback for data that never existed.
async-in-tx.check: Does the forked task read or act on what this transaction writes? Can it run before the commit or after a rollback?

mitigations.name: fork after commit
mitigations.text: the task is submitted from afterCommit, a TransactionSynchronization or an after-commit event listener

mitigations.name: task re-reads with retry
mitigations.text: the task carries only ids and re-reads the rows with a retry that waits for the commit

mitigations.name: tolerates missing row
mitigations.text: the task tolerates a missing row by retrying, but still has external effects on rollback

async-in-tx.cite: the submit line; the @Transactional or transaction start; what the task reads
async-in-tx.fix: Submit the task after the commit (TransactionSynchronization.afterCommit or @TransactionalEventListener) and pass only ids.
async-in-tx.verify: Force a rollback after the submit; the task must not act on the rolled-back data.

dual-write-in-tx.hypothesis: A message is sent inside the database transaction, before the commit; if the commit fails, consumers already received a message about data that does not exist.
dual-write-in-tx.check: Is the send inside the commit scope? What does a consumer do with a message whose data was rolled back? Can a retry of the caller send a second message?

mitigations.name: send after commit
mitigations.text: the send happens in afterCommit or an after-commit event listener

mitigations.name: transactional outbox
mitigations.text: the message is written to an outbox table in the same transaction and relayed later

mitigations.name: event publication registry
mitigations.text: Spring Modulith's event publication registry persists the event with the transaction

mitigations.name: consumer idempotent on business key
mitigations.text: the consumer ignores messages whose data does not exist or was already processed

dual-write-in-tx.cite: the send line; the write line; the transaction boundary
dual-write-in-tx.fix: Write the message to an outbox table in the same transaction and relay it after the commit, or send it from an after-commit hook.
dual-write-in-tx.verify: Force the commit to fail after the send; no consumer may act on the message.

dual-write.hypothesis: The database write and the message send are separate steps; a crash between them keeps one and loses the other.
dual-write.check: Which comes first, the write or the send? Write first: a crash loses the message; send first: consumers hear about a row that is never written. Who notices either? Is there a reconciliation?

mitigations.name: transactional outbox
mitigations.text: the message is written to an outbox table with the data and relayed later

mitigations.name: change data capture
mitigations.text: messages are produced from the database log, not by this code

mitigations.name: idempotent write on redelivery
mitigations.text: the send comes first and the write is idempotent when the work is redelivered

mitigations.name: reconciliation job
mitigations.text: a scheduled job compares the two sides and repairs differences

mitigations.name: consumer tolerates missing message
mitigations.text: the consumer side re-derives state, so a lost message only delays it

dual-write.cite: the write line; the send line
dual-write.fix: Use a transactional outbox, or make one side re-derivable and reconcile it on a schedule.
dual-write.verify: Stop the JVM between the write and the send; the system must converge without manual repair.

remote-in-tx.hypothesis: A remote call happens while a database transaction is open; a rollback afterwards cannot undo what the remote side did, and a slow provider holds connections. For a read, the cost is the held connection, not consistency.
remote-in-tx.check: Is the call a read or an operation with effects? Is the transaction really open at the call? Is the remote effect reversed when the transaction rolls back?

mitigations.name: call outside transaction
mitigations.text: the call actually runs outside the transaction (another proxy, REQUIRES_NEW ended, or no @Transactional on this path)

mitigations.name: read-only call with timeout
mitigations.text: the call only reads and has a short timeout

mitigations.name: compensation that reverses
mitigations.text: a rollback triggers a compensation that undoes the remote effect, not one that only logs

mitigations.name: persisted intent
mitigations.text: the intent is persisted before the call and a later step reconciles it

mitigations.name: remote call last and idempotent
mitigations.text: the call is the last step before the commit and is idempotent, so a retry after a failed commit heals the gap

remote-in-tx.cite: the remote call; the transaction boundary; the rollback handling
remote-in-tx.fix: Move the remote call out of the transaction (before it, or after the commit with persisted intent), or add a compensation that really reverses it.
remote-in-tx.verify: Force a rollback after the remote call succeeds; the remote side must end up consistent.

in-memory-state.hypothesis: Business state is kept in a collection or counter of a singleton bean; it is lost on restart and differs between replicas.
in-memory-state.check: Which business fact does the collection hold? Is it also stored durably? What happens on a restart or with a second replica?

mitigations.name: durable copy
mitigations.text: the same fact is written to a durable store in the same method, or restored at startup

mitigations.name: cache with loader
mitigations.text: the collection is a cache with an expiry and a loader from a durable store

mitigations.name: restored on startup
mitigations.text: the state is rebuilt at startup, but changes since the last write are lost

mitigations.name: single replica stated
mitigations.text: the code states the application runs as one instance (recorded as an assumption)

mitigations.name: connection registry with a relay
mitigations.text: the collection holds live connections (WebSocket sessions, emitters) and messages reach the replica holding them through a broker relay or pub/sub

in-memory-state.cite: the write to the collection; the durable write or its absence
in-memory-state.fix: Keep the state in the database or a shared store, and use memory only as a cache in front of it.
in-memory-state.verify: Restart the instance after a change; the state must survive.

shared-field-write.hypothesis: A request or message writes a field of a singleton bean; concurrent requests overwrite each other and the value differs between replicas.
shared-field-write.check: Is the field per-request data, or configuration set once? Can two requests interleave between the write and the read?

mitigations.name: assigned once
mitigations.text: the field is assigned once from configuration or at startup

mitigations.name: request or session scope
mitigations.text: the bean is request-, session- or prototype-scoped

mitigations.name: synchronized local use
mitigations.text: writes and reads are synchronized and the value is only used within the same call

mitigations.name: refreshed snapshot
mitigations.text: the field holds a derived value that a scheduler or cache refreshes as a whole (a volatile snapshot of configuration, rates or a token)

shared-field-write.cite: the field write; the bean's scope declaration
shared-field-write.fix: Keep per-request data in local variables or method parameters, not in fields of a singleton.
shared-field-write.verify: Send two concurrent requests with different data; each must see only its own.

http-session.hypothesis: Data lives in the in-memory HTTP session; users lose it on a restart or when routed to another replica.
http-session.check: What is stored in the session? What happens when it is missing on another replica?

mitigations.name: spring session
mitigations.text: Spring Session stores the session in a shared store for this module

mitigations.name: cache of durable value
mitigations.text: the attribute only caches a value that is also stored durably

mitigations.name: missing state handled
mitigations.text: the code handles a missing attribute safely by asking the user again

mitigations.name: sticky sessions
mitigations.text: the load balancer keeps each user on one replica (recorded as an assumption); a restart still loses the session

http-session.cite: the session write; the read that depends on it
http-session.fix: Store the session in a shared store (Spring Session) or keep the state on the client or in the database.
http-session.verify: Restart the instance mid-flow; the user's flow must continue or restart safely.

local-file.hypothesis: A file is written to the instance's local disk and read later or by another instance; it is lost when the instance is replaced.
local-file.check: Is the file a staging buffer deleted in the same request, or is it read later or by another instance?

mitigations.name: temp file deleted
mitigations.text: the file is temporary and deleted in a finally block of the same flow

mitigations.name: uploaded in same flow
mitigations.text: the file is uploaded to shared storage within the same flow before it is needed again

mitigations.name: shared volume
mitigations.text: the path is configured as a shared, mounted volume (recorded as an assumption)

mitigations.name: rebuildable cache
mitigations.text: the file is a cache rebuilt on a miss (templates, compiled reports, fonts)

local-file.cite: the file write; the read or delete
local-file.fix: Write to shared object storage, or delete the local file before the flow ends.
local-file.verify: Replace the instance between the write and the read; the flow must still find the data.

consumer-not-idempotent.hypothesis: Brokers deliver at least once and nothing checks whether a message was already processed; a redelivery repeats the write, send or call.
consumer-not-idempotent.check: Can a message be identified (an id or business key)? Is there a unique constraint, a conditional write or a lookup on it before the first side effect? Using the id is not checking it. What exactly is duplicated on redelivery?

mitigations.name: unique business key
mitigations.text: a unique constraint on a business key with conflict handling stops the duplicate

mitigations.name: processed-message table
mitigations.text: a processed-message record is checked before the work

mitigations.name: conditional update
mitigations.text: the write is a conditional update or upsert that is a no-op the second time

mitigations.name: fifo deduplication
mitigations.text: the queue deduplicates by id for a short window (SQS FIFO, 5 minutes)

mitigations.name: message id as primary key
mitigations.text: the row written is keyed by the message id or the payload's business id, so a redelivered insert fails or upserts

mitigations.name: transactional consume and produce
mitigations.text: a Kafka transaction or a transacted JMS session commits the acknowledgement with the work, which removes duplicates from crashes but not from producer retries

consumer-not-idempotent.cite: the listener entry; the first side effect; the check or its absence
consumer-not-idempotent.fix: Record the message id (or business key) with a unique constraint in the same transaction as the work, and skip duplicates.
consumer-not-idempotent.verify: Deliver the same message twice; the side effects must happen once.

webhook-not-idempotent.hypothesis: Providers retry webhooks, and nothing checks the provider's event id; a retry repeats the side effects.
webhook-not-idempotent.check: Which provider id identifies the delivery? Is it checked before the work, or protected by a unique constraint? What is duplicated?

mitigations.name: unique event id
mitigations.text: a unique constraint on the provider event id with conflict handling stops the duplicate

mitigations.name: lookup before write
mitigations.text: the code looks up the event id before doing the work and skips known ones

mitigations.name: harmless duplicates
mitigations.text: duplicates only cost storage, and everything downstream is idempotent

webhook-not-idempotent.cite: the handler entry; the first side effect; the id check or its absence
webhook-not-idempotent.fix: Store the provider event id with a unique constraint in the same transaction as the work, and return success for duplicates.
webhook-not-idempotent.verify: Send the same event twice; the side effects must happen once.

webhook-sync-remote.hypothesis: The webhook calls another service before answering; a slow dependency makes the provider time out and retry while the first attempt still runs.
webhook-sync-remote.check: How long can the remote call take? Does the provider retry while the first attempt runs, and is the handler idempotent?

mitigations.name: short timeout and idempotent handler
mitigations.text: the remote call has a short timeout and the handler is idempotent on the event id

mitigations.name: fetch back by event id
mitigations.text: the remote call fetches the event back from the provider by id with a short timeout, the verification the provider recommends

webhook-sync-remote.cite: the remote call; its timeout configuration or absence
webhook-sync-remote.fix: Acknowledge after persisting the event, and make the remote call from a durable, retried step.
webhook-sync-remote.verify: Delay the remote side beyond the provider's timeout; the work must happen once.

job-without-lock.hypothesis: A scheduled job runs on every instance; with more than one replica it repeats its writes and sends.
job-without-lock.check: With two replicas, what is duplicated? Are the steps row-locked or idempotent? Selecting rows by status is not a claim: it needs FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED or a conditional update whose row count is checked.

mitigations.name: distributed lock
mitigations.text: ShedLock, a Quartz JDBC store or leader election guards the job, through code the scanner missed

mitigations.name: row claim or upsert
mitigations.text: every write claims rows (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) or is an upsert

mitigations.name: idempotent by comment
mitigations.text: comments state the steps are idempotent, without code that enforces it

mitigations.name: one scheduling deployment
mitigations.text: a profile or property enables the job in one deployment only (@Profile, @ConditionalOnProperty, spring.task.scheduling.enabled), recorded as an assumption about the replica count

mitigations.name: clustered Quartz
mitigations.text: the job is a Quartz job with @DisallowConcurrentExecution on a clustered JDBC job store

job-without-lock.cite: the @Scheduled method; the first write or send; the lock or its absence
job-without-lock.fix: Guard the job with ShedLock or a database lock, or make each step claim its rows.
job-without-lock.verify: Run two instances at the scheduled time; the work must happen once.

proxy-bypassed.hypothesis: A method calls its own @Async or @Transactional method through this; the proxy never sees the call, so it runs synchronously or without the transaction.
proxy-bypassed.check: Which annotation is bypassed? Does it matter here (@Async always; @Transactional only when the target writes or sends)?

mitigations.name: self-injected proxy
mitigations.text: the call goes through a self-injected proxy or AopContext.currentProxy()

mitigations.name: caller transactional
mitigations.text: the caller is itself transactional, so the work still runs in a transaction

mitigations.name: AspectJ mode
mitigations.text: transactions or async run in AspectJ mode (mode = AdviceMode.ASPECTJ), which also intercepts calls through this

proxy-bypassed.cite: the self-call; the annotation on the target
proxy-bypassed.fix: Move the annotated method to another bean, or call it through the proxy.
proxy-bypassed.verify: Assert in a test that the target runs on another thread or in a transaction.

async-listener.hypothesis: An event listener runs asynchronously; the event exists only in memory until it runs, so a restart drops it.
async-listener.check: Is the listener's work required? Is the event persisted anywhere?

mitigations.name: event publication registry
mitigations.text: Spring Modulith's event publication registry persists the event

mitigations.name: re-derivable by sweeper
mitigations.text: a sweeper re-derives the listener's work from durable state

mitigations.name: best-effort listener
mitigations.text: the listener's work is best effort by the code's own statement

async-listener.fix: Persist the event (outbox or Modulith registry) or make the work re-derivable.
async-listener.verify: Stop the JVM after publishing; the listener's work must still happen.

handoff-in-listener.hypothesis: A listener hands work to an in-process thread and returns; if the instance stops before the work runs, it is lost.
handoff-in-listener.check: Is the forked work required? Does anything re-derive it?

mitigations.name: durable claim before fork
mitigations.text: the work is persisted with a claimable state and a sweeper picks it up

handoff-in-listener.cite: the submit line; the listener method
handoff-in-listener.fix: Do the work in the listener, or persist it and process it with a sweeper.
handoff-in-listener.verify: Stop the JVM before the forked task runs; the work must still happen.

handoff-in-job.hypothesis: A scheduled job forks work onto other threads; a shutdown drops what is still queued, and the next run may not pick it up.
handoff-in-job.check: What is queued when a shutdown hits? Does the next run pick it up?

mitigations.name: re-derived every run
mitigations.text: the job re-derives its work from durable state on every run

mitigations.name: drains on shutdown
mitigations.text: the executor waits for queued tasks on shutdown

handoff-in-job.cite: the submit line; how the job selects its work
handoff-in-job.fix: Select work from durable state on every run and mark it done only after it completes.
handoff-in-job.verify: Stop the JVM mid-run; the next run must finish the work.

notification-in-tx.hypothesis: A notification goes out from another thread while the transaction is still open; users can be told about a change that rolls back.
notification-in-tx.check: Can the user be told about a change that later rolls back? Is that acceptable for this notification?

mitigations.name: sent after commit
mitigations.text: the notification is sent after the commit

mitigations.name: best-effort notification
mitigations.text: the notification is informational and a wrong one is harmless

notification-in-tx.cite: the notification submit; the transaction boundary
notification-in-tx.fix: Send the notification after the commit.
notification-in-tx.verify: Force a rollback after the notification is queued; no user may be notified.

notification-handoff.hypothesis: A message to users (e-mail, SMS, chat) is sent on another thread after the work returns; a restart loses the ones still queued.
notification-handoff.check: Must the user get this notification, or is it best effort? If the forked work also writes business rows or moves money, it is business work, not a notification. Is it recorded durably before the hand-off? Does anything resend a lost one?

mitigations.name: persisted notification
mitigations.text: the notification is stored (an outbox row or a queue message) before the hand-off, and a job or consumer sends it

mitigations.name: send awaited
mitigations.text: the future of the send is joined or awaited before the work returns

mitigations.name: best-effort by owner
mitigations.text: the code states the notification is best effort (a comment, a name or a log that says so)

notification-handoff.cite: the hand-off line; the send; the durable record or its absence
notification-handoff.fix: Store the notification in the same transaction as the change and send it from a job or a broker consumer, or state that losing it is acceptable.
notification-handoff.verify: Stop the instance right after the operation returns; the notification must still go out, or its loss must be accepted.

timer-handoff.hypothesis: Work is scheduled to run later on an in-process timer; if the instance restarts before it fires, the work never happens.
timer-handoff.check: Does the delayed work matter to the business? Is the due work stored anywhere durable? Does a startup hook or a scheduled job pick up what was missed?

mitigations.name: persisted schedule
mitigations.text: the due work is stored with its time, and a scheduled job or a startup hook runs what is due

mitigations.name: re-derived on startup
mitigations.text: a startup hook or a scheduled job re-derives the pending work from durable state

mitigations.name: best-effort by owner
mitigations.text: the code states the delayed work is best effort, such as a cache refresh or a reminder that may be skipped

timer-handoff.cite: the schedule call; where the due work is stored, or its absence
timer-handoff.fix: Store the due work with its time and run it from a scheduled job or a persistent scheduler (Quartz with a JDBC store, db-scheduler, JobRunr).
timer-handoff.verify: Schedule the work, restart the instance before it fires; it must still run.

async-response.hypothesis: The handler returns a Mono, future or emitter and the client waits; a restart fails the request, and a client that retries may repeat work the first attempt already did.
async-response.check: Does the asynchronous work write, send or call out? Can a retried request repeat that? Is the work durable before the response completes?

mitigations.name: reads only
mitigations.text: the asynchronous work only reads; a retry repeats nothing

mitigations.name: idempotent by key
mitigations.text: writes and sends are keyed by a request or business id, so a retried request does not repeat them

mitigations.name: durable before response
mitigations.text: the work is committed before the response completes, so a failed response leaves a consistent state

async-response.cite: the returned future or publisher; the writes and sends it performs; the key or check that makes a retry safe, or its absence
async-response.fix: Make the asynchronous writes idempotent by a request id, or commit the work before completing the response.
async-response.verify: Kill the instance while the request is in flight, retry it; the end state must match one successful request.

background-thread.hypothesis: A thread or recurring task started at startup or shutdown does work that a restart interrupts; work in flight is lost or repeated.
background-thread.check: What does the thread do: housekeeping or business work? Is it stopped cleanly on shutdown? Is its work reconstructed from durable state after a restart?

mitigations.name: housekeeping only
mitigations.text: the work is per-instance housekeeping (metrics, cache refresh, connection keep-alive) whose loss changes no business state

mitigations.name: work is durable
mitigations.text: the work it processes is read from durable state and marked done there, so a restart resumes it

mitigations.name: stopped on shutdown
mitigations.text: the thread or executor is shut down and drained in @PreDestroy, SmartLifecycle.stop or a shutdown hook

background-thread.cite: where the thread starts; what it does; how it stops
background-thread.fix: Drive the work from durable state (claimed rows, a queue) and stop the thread cleanly on shutdown.
background-thread.verify: Stop the instance while the thread is working; after restart nothing may be lost or done twice.

in-memory-cache.hypothesis: A cache, counter or lock map lives in instance memory; that is wrong when it is the only copy of a fact, or when replicas must agree on it.
in-memory-cache.check: Is the value derived from a durable source, or is memory its only copy? Do replicas need the same value (rate limits, locks, sequence numbers)?

mitigations.name: derived data
mitigations.text: every value can be recomputed from a durable source, such as a cache with a loader

mitigations.name: shared store
mitigations.text: the structure is backed by a shared store (Redis, Hazelcast, the database)

mitigations.name: single replica stated
mitigations.text: the code states the application runs as one instance (recorded as an assumption)

in-memory-cache.cite: the write to the in-memory structure; its durable source, or its absence
in-memory-cache.fix: Keep facts that matter in a shared store, and use memory only as a cache that can be rebuilt.
in-memory-cache.verify: Run two replicas or restart one; the value must agree or be rebuilt correctly.

event-in-tx.hypothesis: An in-process event is published inside a transaction; plain @EventListener methods run before the commit and may act on data that then rolls back. It is worst when a listener sends, calls out or notifies.
event-in-tx.check: Which listeners handle the event? Do they act outside the transaction (send, call, notify, another data source)? Do they run before the commit?

mitigations.name: after-commit listeners
mitigations.text: every listener of the event is a @TransactionalEventListener after commit, or registers its work after the commit

mitigations.name: same transaction only
mitigations.text: the listeners only change data inside the same transaction, which rolls back with it

mitigations.name: idempotent reaction
mitigations.text: the listener's outside effect is checked or keyed, so acting on a rolled-back change is harmless

event-in-tx.cite: the publish; the transaction boundary; each listener's outside effect
event-in-tx.fix: Handle the event with @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT), or publish it through an outbox.
event-in-tx.verify: Force a rollback after the publish; no listener may have acted outside the transaction.

read-verb-writes.hypothesis: A GET or HEAD request writes or sends; clients, proxies and crawlers retry and prefetch these freely, so the write repeats.
read-verb-writes.check: What does the write change? Is it the same on every call? Could a crawler or a prefetch trigger it?

mitigations.name: same result on repeat
mitigations.text: the write sets the same value on every call (an upsert of the same row), so a repeat changes nothing

mitigations.name: access record only
mitigations.text: the write only records the access (audit log, last-seen time), where repeats are harmless

read-verb-writes.cite: the HTTP verb; the write or send
read-verb-writes.fix: Move the change to a POST, PUT or PATCH, or make it idempotent.
read-verb-writes.verify: Call the GET twice; the state must not change the second time.

after-commit-listener-writes-db.hypothesis: An after-commit listener writes to the database without a new transaction; the write joins the committed transaction still bound to the thread, so it is never flushed or committed and is silently lost.
after-commit-listener-writes-db.check: Is the listener synchronous (no @Async)? Does the writing method run in REQUIRES_NEW through a proxy? Is the write a JPA change, which waits for a flush that never comes?

mitigations.name: REQUIRES_NEW
mitigations.text: the writing method runs in @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW) through a proxy, or a TransactionTemplate set to REQUIRES_NEW

mitigations.name: runs on another thread
mitigations.text: the listener is @Async or an @ApplicationModuleListener, so no committed transaction is bound to its thread

mitigations.name: auto-commit JDBC
mitigations.text: the write is a plain JDBC statement on a connection that commits it by itself

after-commit-listener-writes-db.cite: the listener annotation and its phase; the write; the transaction declaration of the writing method, or its absence
after-commit-listener-writes-db.fix: Run the listener's writes in a REQUIRES_NEW transaction, or make the listener asynchronous and its work durable.
after-commit-listener-writes-db.verify: Publish the event and commit, then read the listener's row from another connection; it must exist.

after-commit-listener-without-transactio.hypothesis: The event is published outside any transaction and a listener of it is a @TransactionalEventListener without fallbackExecution; Spring skips that listener silently, so its work never happens.
after-commit-listener-without-transactio.check: Is a transaction open where the event is published, perhaps through a caller or a TransactionTemplate the path shows? Does every after-commit listener of the event set fallbackExecution?

mitigations.name: fallbackExecution
mitigations.text: the listener declares fallbackExecution = true

mitigations.name: published inside a transaction
mitigations.text: the publish runs inside a transaction after all: a TransactionTemplate callback or a transactional caller on this path

after-commit-listener-without-transactio.cite: the publish and the transaction state around it; the listener annotation
after-commit-listener-without-transactio.fix: Publish the event inside the transaction that makes the change, or set fallbackExecution = true when no transaction is intended.
after-commit-listener-without-transactio.verify: Call the operation and check that the listener's work happened.

read-only-tx-writes.hypothesis: A write runs inside a read-only transaction; Hibernate does not flush changed entities there and a read-only connection rejects the statement, so the change is lost or the call fails.
read-only-tx-writes.check: Is the transaction at the write really readOnly (on the method or its class)? Is the write a JPA entity change, a save of a new entity, or a native statement? Does a read-write transaction open in between?

mitigations.name: read-write transaction inside
mitigations.text: a method between the read-only boundary and the write opens its own read-write transaction (REQUIRES_NEW through a proxy)

mitigations.name: misnamed read
mitigations.text: the repository method only reads despite its name

mitigations.name: native statement
mitigations.text: the write is a @Modifying query or JDBC statement, which runs regardless of the flush mode unless the connection is read-only

read-only-tx-writes.cite: the write line; the @Transactional(readOnly = true) that encloses it
read-only-tx-writes.fix: Give the writing method its own read-write @Transactional, or drop readOnly from the boundary.
read-only-tx-writes.verify: Run the operation and read the row from another connection; the change must be there.

lock-held-across-remote-call.hypothesis: The transaction locks rows and then waits for a remote service; every other writer of those rows waits as long as the provider does, and a hung provider turns into lock timeouts across the system.
lock-held-across-remote-call.check: Which row lock is held at the remote call? Is the lock still held there (same transaction)? Does the call have a short timeout? Is the lock meant to serialise calls per row?

mitigations.name: call after the lock is released
mitigations.text: the remote call runs after the locking transaction committed, in another transaction or after commit

mitigations.name: intended per-row guard with timeout
mitigations.text: the lock deliberately serialises calls for one row and the call has a timeout of a few seconds

lock-held-across-remote-call.cite: the locking query; the remote call; the transaction boundary that spans both
lock-held-across-remote-call.fix: Persist the intent under the lock, commit, then call the provider from a retried step; at least bound the call with a short timeout.
lock-held-across-remote-call.verify: Make the provider slow; operations on the same rows must not wait for it.

flush-on-shutdown.hypothesis: Shutdown code writes, sends or calls out; on a kill, an out-of-memory crash or an expired grace period it never runs, so whatever it was meant to save is lost.
flush-on-shutdown.check: What does the hook write or send? Was the same data already stored when it was produced? What is lost if the hook does not run?

mitigations.name: housekeeping only
mitigations.text: the hook only closes clients, deregisters or logs; no business data depends on it

mitigations.name: persisted when produced
mitigations.text: the data is already stored durably when produced, and the hook only speeds up a flush

mitigations.name: short periodic flush
mitigations.text: a scheduled flush runs every few seconds, so only the last interval is at risk

flush-on-shutdown.cite: the shutdown hook; the write or send in it; where the data was produced and whether it was stored then
flush-on-shutdown.fix: Persist the data when it is produced and treat the shutdown hook as an optimisation.
flush-on-shutdown.verify: Kill the JVM with SIGKILL during activity; nothing that matters to the business may be lost.

startup-remote-call.hypothesis: Startup calls a remote service and waits for it; when the dependency is down at deploy time the application fails or hangs before it is ready, so a partner outage blocks every deploy and restart.
startup-remote-call.check: What happens when the call fails or hangs: does startup fail, wait or carry on? Does the call have a timeout? Is the result needed before serving traffic?

mitigations.name: fails open
mitigations.text: a failure is caught and the application starts with defaults or retries later

mitigations.name: runs after readiness on a thread
mitigations.text: the call runs on a background thread after the application is ready

mitigations.name: bounded retry with timeout
mitigations.text: the call has a short timeout and a capped retry, after which startup carries on

startup-remote-call.cite: the startup hook; the remote call; its timeout and error handling
startup-remote-call.fix: Make startup independent of the dependency: load lazily on first use, or warm up after readiness with retries.
startup-remote-call.verify: Start the application with the dependency unreachable; it must become ready.

quartz-concurrent-execution.hypothesis: A Quartz job that writes or sends has no @DisallowConcurrentExecution; a run that outlasts its interval, or a misfire, overlaps the previous one and repeats its effects.
quartz-concurrent-execution.check: Can a run outlast the trigger interval? What does an overlapping run duplicate? Does each run claim its rows?

mitigations.name: row claims
mitigations.text: every write claims rows (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, or a conditional update whose row count is checked)

mitigations.name: idempotent steps
mitigations.text: every step is an upsert or a conditional update, so a second run changes nothing

mitigations.name: interval far longer than runs
mitigations.text: the trigger interval is far longer than any run (recorded as an assumption)

quartz-concurrent-execution.cite: the Job class and its annotations; the first write or send
quartz-concurrent-execution.fix: Annotate the job with @DisallowConcurrentExecution, and @PersistJobDataAfterExecution when it keeps progress in the JobDataMap.
quartz-concurrent-execution.verify: Make one run slower than the trigger interval; only one execution may be active.

consumer-swallows-failure.hypothesis: A catch on the consumer's path takes the exception, logs it and returns; the message is acknowledged and never redelivered, so the failed work is gone with only a log line left.
consumer-swallows-failure.check: What does the catch enclose? What does it do besides logging: rethrow, nack, change visibility, write a failure row, send to a dead-letter destination? Is the swallowed work business work?

mitigations.name: rethrown
mitigations.text: the catch rethrows, possibly wrapped, so the container retries or dead-letters the message

mitigations.name: negative acknowledgement
mitigations.text: the catch nacks, rejects or changes the message visibility

mitigations.name: failure persisted
mitigations.text: the catch stores the message in a failed-messages table or sends it to a dead-letter destination

mitigations.name: best-effort side call
mitigations.text: the swallowed call is a side effect the code calls best effort, and the main work fails normally

consumer-swallows-failure.cite: the try and catch lines; what the catch does; the work inside the try
consumer-swallows-failure.fix: Let the exception reach the container's error handler with retries and a dead-letter destination, or persist the failure before acknowledging.
consumer-swallows-failure.verify: Make the processing throw; the message must be redelivered or land in the dead-letter destination.

http-client-without-timeout.hypothesis: The HTTP client used on this path has no connect or read timeout; a partner that accepts the connection and never answers pins the calling thread, its transaction and its listener forever.
http-client-without-timeout.check: How is the client built? Are connect and read or response timeouts set on it, on its request factory or connector, or by spring.http.client properties? Does a time limiter bound the call?

mitigations.name: timeouts on the factory
mitigations.text: a request factory, HttpClient or connector with connect and read timeouts is given to the client

mitigations.name: client settings in config
mitigations.text: spring.http.client connect and read timeouts, or a client settings bean, apply to this client

mitigations.name: time limiter
mitigations.text: a time limiter or a future timeout bounds every use of the client

http-client-without-timeout.cite: the client construction; the timeout or factory calls, or their absence; one call through the client
http-client-without-timeout.fix: Build the client from a request factory with explicit connect and read timeouts of seconds, and share it.
http-client-without-timeout.verify: Point the client at a server that accepts and never answers; the call must fail within the timeout.

remote-failure-swallowed.hypothesis: A remote call or a message send is wrapped in a catch that only logs; the operation succeeds anyway, the side effect never happens and nothing retries or records it.
remote-failure-swallowed.check: What does the catch do besides logging? Is the failed effect recorded as pending or failed anywhere? Does a job or a reconciliation redo it? Is the effect required, or best effort?

mitigations.name: failure recorded for retry
mitigations.text: the catch writes a pending or failed status, an outbox row or a dead-letter message that a job retries

mitigations.name: rethrown after cleanup
mitigations.text: the catch rethrows after compensating

mitigations.name: still pending for the next run
mitigations.text: the failed item stays pending, such as an outbox row left unsent, and the next run of the job retries it

mitigations.name: best-effort by owner
mitigations.text: the code states the effect is best effort, such as a metric push

mitigations.name: reconciliation
mitigations.text: a scheduled job compares the two systems and repairs what is missing

remote-failure-swallowed.cite: the try and catch; the remote call or send inside; what the catch writes or sends
remote-failure-swallowed.fix: Persist the intent before the call and let a retried step perform it, or fail the operation when the effect is required.
remote-failure-swallowed.verify: Make the dependency fail; the effect must happen later, or the operation must report the failure.

send-result-ignored.hypothesis: The send returns a future, a Mono or a flag that nothing reads; a rejected or timed-out message is at most logged while the caller reports success, so the message is lost without an error.
send-result-ignored.check: Is the result joined, chained with a callback or checked anywhere? Has the caller already committed or answered when the send fails? For a Mono, is it subscribed at all?

mitigations.name: result handled
mitigations.text: the future is joined before returning, or a callback records the failure durably

mitigations.name: outbox relay
mitigations.text: the send belongs to an outbox relay that marks the row sent only after the future completes

mitigations.name: producer listener
mitigations.text: a producer listener or an error channel logs and counts failed sends without recovering them

send-result-ignored.cite: the send line; the result that nothing reads; the caller's commit or answer
send-result-ignored.fix: Wait for the send before committing or answering, or send from an outbox relay that marks rows sent on success.
send-result-ignored.verify: Make the broker reject the send; the caller must fail, or the message must stay pending for a retry.

executor-unbounded-queue.hypothesis: The executor that takes this work has an unbounded queue or unbounded threads, or drops its queue on shutdown; a burst fills the heap until the replica is killed with every queued task, and a deploy loses what is queued.
executor-unbounded-queue.check: How is the executor built: queue capacity, thread limit, rejection policy, wait for tasks on shutdown? Is it the executor the hand-off on this path uses?

mitigations.name: bounded queue with policy
mitigations.text: the queue has a capacity and a rejection policy that pushes back on the caller or persists the work

mitigations.name: another executor
mitigations.text: the hand-off on this path uses a different, bounded executor than the one flagged

mitigations.name: low task volume
mitigations.text: the executor receives a few tasks per minute from one job

executor-unbounded-queue.cite: the executor construction; the queue capacity and shutdown settings, or their absence; the hand-off that uses it
executor-unbounded-queue.fix: Bound the queue and threads, choose a rejection policy that pushes back, wait for tasks on shutdown, and persist work that must not be lost.
executor-unbounded-queue.verify: Submit tasks faster than they complete; memory must stay bounded and callers must feel back-pressure.

nested-requires-new-in-tx.hypothesis: A REQUIRES_NEW method is called while another transaction holds a connection; each such thread needs two pooled connections at once, which deadlocks the pool under load, and the inner commit survives an outer rollback.
nested-requires-new-in-tx.check: Is the outer transaction open at the call? Must the inner work survive an outer rollback (an audit row), or is it business data that should roll back too? Can the inner step run after the outer commit instead?

mitigations.name: outer transaction already ended
mitigations.text: the inner method runs after the outer commit (an after-commit hook, another thread)

mitigations.name: intended audit row with a sized pool
mitigations.text: the inner transaction writes an audit or log row that must survive a rollback, and the pool is sized for two connections per thread

nested-requires-new-in-tx.cite: the REQUIRES_NEW declaration; the outer @Transactional; the call between them
nested-requires-new-in-tx.fix: Run the inner step after the outer commit, or let it join the outer transaction; if it must stay, size the pool for two connections per thread.
nested-requires-new-in-tx.verify: Run as many concurrent calls as the pool has connections; none may time out waiting for a connection.

request-answers-ok-on-failure.hypothesis: The handler catches the failure and returns normally, so the caller gets a success status; a client or webhook provider that would retry an error never does, and work done before the failure stays half finished.
request-answers-ok-on-failure.check: What status and body go back on the catch path? Was the request stored durably before the failing step? Does the only client read an error code from the body?

mitigations.name: request persisted before the answer
mitigations.text: the request was stored durably before the failing step, so success is the right answer and a job finishes the work

mitigations.name: error status set elsewhere
mitigations.text: the error status is set by an exception handler or a response object the catch fills

mitigations.name: error code checked by client
mitigations.text: the success body carries an error code that the only client handles

request-answers-ok-on-failure.cite: the catch; the status or body it returns; the work before the failing step
request-answers-ok-on-failure.fix: Answer an error status so the client retries, or store the request before answering success and finish it from a retried step.
request-answers-ok-on-failure.verify: Make the work throw; the client must get an error status, or the work must complete later.

graceful-shutdown-off.hypothesis: The web server is not shut down gracefully; on every deploy, scale-in or node drain it stops at once, so requests in flight are cut half done and clients see errors they may retry.
graceful-shutdown-off.check: Is server.shutdown set to graceful in any production config the packet names, or does the Spring Boot version shut down gracefully by default (3.4 and later)? Is the application deployed as a WAR on an external server, where this key does not apply?

mitigations.name: graceful in another file
mitigations.text: a production profile file or an environment-specific config sets server.shutdown=graceful

mitigations.name: Boot default
mitigations.text: the project runs Spring Boot 3.4 or later, where graceful shutdown is the default

mitigations.name: external server
mitigations.text: the application is deployed as a WAR, so the external server's shutdown applies

mitigations.name: drain before stop
mitigations.text: the deployment removes the instance from the load balancer and waits before stopping it (a preStop sleep), recorded as an assumption

graceful-shutdown-off.cite: the config line, or the config file and Spring Boot version that show the key is missing
graceful-shutdown-off.fix: Set server.shutdown=graceful and spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase above the longest request, and give the pod a matching termination grace period.
graceful-shutdown-off.verify: Send SIGTERM during a slow request; it must complete and new requests must be refused.

open-in-view-enabled.hypothesis: Open Session in View is on, so each web request keeps its persistence context and its database connection until the response is written; a remote call made after the transaction holds a pooled connection for its whole duration.
open-in-view-enabled.check: Is spring.jpa.open-in-view set to false in a production config the packet names? Does this operation call out after reading from the database, outside a transaction?

mitigations.name: disabled in another file
mitigations.text: a production config sets spring.jpa.open-in-view=false

mitigations.name: no call after database access
mitigations.text: the operation's remote calls happen before it touches the database, so the connection is not yet taken

open-in-view-enabled.cite: the config line, or the config file that shows the key is missing; one remote call of the operation
open-in-view-enabled.fix: Set spring.jpa.open-in-view=false and load what views need inside the transaction.
open-in-view-enabled.verify: Make the remote service slow and send concurrent requests; the database pool must not run dry.

kafka-auto-commit.hypothesis: Kafka offsets are committed automatically on a timer, whether or not the listener finished; a crash between the commit and the end of processing loses those messages.
kafka-auto-commit.check: Is enable-auto-commit really true for this consumer's factory, or does a container factory in code override it? Is the listener's work idempotent if the setting is changed to manual commits?

mitigations.name: overridden in code
mitigations.text: a consumer factory in code sets ENABLE_AUTO_COMMIT_CONFIG to false for this listener

mitigations.name: loss accepted
mitigations.text: the topic carries data the owner accepts to lose, such as metrics or telemetry

kafka-auto-commit.cite: the config line that enables auto commit; the listener
kafka-auto-commit.fix: Set enable-auto-commit=false and let the listener container commit after processing (the default ack mode), with retries and a dead-letter topic.
kafka-auto-commit.verify: Kill the consumer while it processes a batch; after a restart every message must be processed.

ddl-auto-in-production.hypothesis: Hibernate creates or alters tables at startup in a production config; schema changes happen unreviewed during deploys, while replicas still run the old code, and create or create-drop wipe data.
ddl-auto-in-production.check: Is the setting in a file production uses, or only in a local profile? Is the value update, create or create-drop? Does a migration tool own the schema as well?

mitigations.name: local profile only
mitigations.text: the setting is in a profile used only for local runs or tests, and production sets validate or none

mitigations.name: overridden at deploy
mitigations.text: the deployment overrides the value through an environment variable, recorded as an assumption

ddl-auto-in-production.fix: Set ddl-auto to validate or none in production and own the schema with Flyway or Liquibase migrations.
ddl-auto-in-production.verify: Start the application against a copy of production with an entity change; the schema must not change.

feign-default-timeouts.hypothesis: Feign clients run on their default timeouts: ten seconds to connect and sixty to read; a slow partner ties up the calling thread for a minute per call, and request threads run out.
feign-default-timeouts.check: Do the production configs the packet names set connect and read timeouts for these clients, by default or per client? Does a Request.Options bean or a time limiter in code set them?

mitigations.name: timeouts in another file
mitigations.text: a production config sets spring.cloud.openfeign.client.config default or per-client timeouts

mitigations.name: options in code
mitigations.text: a Request.Options bean or a Feign builder in code sets connect and read timeouts

mitigations.name: time limiter
mitigations.text: a time limiter or circuit breaker with a short timeout wraps the calls

feign-default-timeouts.cite: the config file that lacks the timeouts; one Feign call
feign-default-timeouts.fix: Set spring.cloud.openfeign.client.config.default.connect-timeout and read-timeout to a few seconds, and tighter per client where needed.
feign-default-timeouts.verify: Make the partner answer after 30 seconds; the call must fail within the configured timeout.

destructive-migration.hypothesis: The newest migration drops, renames or retypes a column or table that this operation writes; during a rolling deploy the replicas still on the old code fail against the new schema.
destructive-migration.check: Does the old code still read or write what the statement changes? Is the change split into expand and contract steps across releases? Has this migration been deployed already?

mitigations.name: expand and contract
mitigations.text: the code that used the column was removed in an earlier release, so no running replica needs it

mitigations.name: deploy without old replicas
mitigations.text: the deploy stops every old replica before migrating (recreate strategy), accepting downtime

mitigations.name: already deployed
mitigations.text: this migration is already applied in production, so the next deploy does not run it

destructive-migration.cite: the destructive statement; the write of this operation that touches the same table
destructive-migration.fix: Split the change: add the new shape first, deploy code that uses both, then drop the old one in a later release.
destructive-migration.verify: Run the old and the new version side by side against the migrated schema; both must keep working.

no-hint.hypothesis: The scan matched no failure pattern on this operation, although it writes, sends or calls out. A rule may have missed one.
no-hint.check: Read the entry method and the listed effects. Is the caller answered before the work is durable? Can a retry or redelivery repeat a write, send or call? Is a remote call or send inside a transaction? Can a crash split a write from a send? Is a fact kept only in memory?
no-hint.cite: the lines that show the failure, or the lines that make the path safe
no-hint.fix: Fix it as the named rule's task says.
no-hint.verify: Verify it as the named rule's task says.
